title: Partner Pen Play in Parallel (PPPiP): A New Paradigm for Relationship Improvement

abstract: Healthy romantic relationships contribute to human physical health and emotional well-being. Here we introduce Partner Pen Play in Parallel (PPPiP), the act of simultaneous improvisational drawing on paper without clinical supervision. We provide interdisciplinary evidence from art therapy, sexology, affective neuroscience, and aesthetics to support PPPiP as a useful strategy for relationship development. methods.name: Definition and practice description of Partner Pen Play in Parallel
methods.description: Specifies PPPiP as two people simultaneously drawing on one sheet with pens, and outlines how sessions begin, proceed, and end.
methods.evidence: PPPiP is the act of two people simultaneously drawing on one piece of paper. Partners sit across from each other, or side by side if permitted by handedness.

methods.name: Interdisciplinary synthesis from art therapy, sexology, neuroscience, aesthetics
methods.description: In the absence of direct studies, the authors synthesize prior research to argue a plausible scientific basis for PPPiP.
methods.evidence: As there are currently no studies that directly test the neural or psychological efficacy of PPPiP, here we synthesize research from various fields to describe a plausible scientific basis for PPPiP

methods.name: Mapping PPPiP onto Wadeson's five-element art therapy framework
methods.description: Re-enumerates Wadeson's five advantages of art therapy (Immediate, Genuine, Spatial Expression, Permanent, Shared Pleasure) and checks PPPiP against them.
methods.evidence: Wadeson (2010, p. 401) presents five advantageous aspects of art therapy relative to traditional couples therapy.

methods.name: Free Energy Principle framing of partner modeling (FEPPPPiP)
methods.description: Interprets joint drawing as building a generative model of the partner and as collective self-evidencing of the relationship.
methods.evidence: PPPiP is an exercise in strengthening one’s neural representation of a partner.

methods.name: Appendix of example drawings by the authors
methods.description: Presents author-made examples of the two PPPiP categories, fontplay and pure abstraction.
methods.evidence: In the Appendix to this paper, we present several examples of fontplay (Appendix A) and pure abstraction (Appendix B).

key_findings: The authors conclude PPPiP shares all five characteristics hypothesized to make art therapy effective in marital contexts.
They propose a model in which PPPiP synergistically activates motor and cortico-limbic circuits, supported by imaging evidence from improvisational and aesthetic contexts.
PPPiP is distinguished from traditional art therapy as less clinically oriented, with fewer external constraints and direct integration of art-making with relationship co-creation.
The authors predict greater neural synchrony between partners than strangers, and in PPPiP versus isolated tandem drawing, as a testable future direction.
key_findings_evidence: Thus we conclude that PPPiP shares all five of the implicit qualitative characteristics that are hypothesized to make art therapy effective in marital contexts

Evidence from brain imaging in improvisational and aesthetic contexts supports a model in which PPPiP synergistically activates motor and cortico-limbic neural circuits associated with skilled emotive-creative processes.

Relative to traditional art therapy practices, PPPiP is less clinically oriented, features fewer external constraints, and directly encourages the dynamic integration of artistic creation with relationship co-creation.
We predict increased neural synchrony between partners than between strangers in all task cases, and increased neural synchrony in PPPiP conditions versus isolated tandem drawing conditions.
